item.research_question: Can CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy coatings, produced via mechanical alloying and electro spark deposition, provide effective corrosion resistance and adhesion for stainless steel substrates in aggressive geothermal environments?
item.material_system: CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy deposited on 316 L stainless steel substrate
item.processing_route: Solid-state processing: Mechanical alloying of high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Mo powders for 30 h in a Pulverisette 6 Classic Line planetary ball mill (350 RPM, ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, N-Heptane process control agent) under Argon; cold pressing at 250 kN into 25 mm × 5 mm samples; sintering at 1100 °C for 1 h; machining into electrodes; electro spark deposition (ESD) under Argon atmosphere to deposit successive layers.
item.test_conditions: Pull-off testing per ASTM D4541–01; electrochemical corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 ± 0.5 °C for 6 h using potentiodynamic polarization.
key_findings: Maximum adhesion resistance reached 0.67 MPa, limited by epoxy resin failure rather than coating-substrate interface failure.
Corrosion rate of the ESD coating calculated at 0.00016 mm/year in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
Polarization resistance of the coating was higher than 316 L stainless steel (22.50 kΩ × cm2).
XRD analysis revealed an increase in σ phase (rich in Co, Cr, Fe) and μ phase (rich in Mo) in the coating compared to the sintered electrode.
The coating microstructure showed a homogeneous and adhesive layer near the substrate, with slight porosity and splats in the upper part.
After corrosion testing, a passivation layer formed on the surface, covering most pores, containing an oxygen component likely from segregated chromium.
The open circuit potential (Eoc) was more electronegative than the bulk as-cast alloy, attributed to increased porosity delaying passivation.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the phase transformation (increase in σ and μ phases) to the rapid melting and cooling during the electro spark deposition process, driven by temperature differences and local solute solidification. The superior corrosion resistance is explained by the rapid formation of a passivation film, likely containing segregated chromium, which covers surface pores and reduces the corrosion current density significantly compared to bulk alloys or stainless steel.
item.limitations: The coating is slightly porous in the upper part due to the BCC structure prone to pore formation in this high-entropy alloy and the ESD technique; the open circuit potential is more electronegative than the bulk alloy due to this porosity delaying passivation.
item.future_work: The authors state that novel promising coatings resistant to long-term high-temperature oxidation, corrosion action, and wear are currently being sought, implying further development is needed for these specific conditions.
